deals.source: The Bridge Teachers, “Too Strong to Overcall 6.17.24”, board 8
reviewNotes: Hands and auction transcribed from the video's screenshots. Double dummy, NS take 9 tricks in spades: 3♠ makes and 4♠ is one down.

problems.explanation: You have 20 HCP and five good hearts. A simple overcall shows about 8-17, so 1♥ would undersell the hand: partner would pass with a few points, and you'd never show your strength. Double first, then show the rest at your next turn, by raising partner's suit if it fits or bidding your hearts. Double-then-bid shows a hand too strong to overcall.

whyNot.1H: A simple overcall shows about 8-17. Partner, with a weak hand and short hearts, would pass, and you'd never get to show 20 points.
whyNot.1N: A 1NT overcall shows 15-18 balanced. You have 20, and a five-card suit worth showing.

problems.explanation: Partner had to answer your double, so 1♠ shows four or more spades and anything from 0 to about 8 points. You have four-card support and 20 HCP. Because you doubled first, a raise now shows a strong hand, not a minimum takeout double: jump to 3♠ to invite game. Partner bids 4♠ with a few useful points and passes with nothing.

whyNot.2S: After a takeout double, a simple raise shows a minimum double, about 13-16. You have 20.
whyNot.4S: Partner's 1♠ was forced and may hold nothing. Here it's one down double dummy: 3♠ is the limit opposite this hand.
whyNot.2H: You have a spade fit. Showing it describes your hand better than a second suit.

deals.source: The Bridge Teachers, “Too Strong to Overcall 2.10.25”, board 1
deals.unusualSetup: The video deals board 1 with East as dealer.
reviewNotes: Hands and auction transcribed from the video's screenshots. Double dummy, 6♠ makes.
South has 13 HCP, so this goes beyond the agreement's '17+': the hand is too strong by playing tricks (eight spades to the AKJ10, about nine tricks), not points.
North's 5♥ is a control bid in the opponents' suit, the idea set aside on control-3, so only South's first two calls are drilled.

problems.explanation: Only 13 HCP, but eight spades to the AKJ10 and the ♦A: about nine tricks on your own. Jump overcalls are weak, and a simple 1♠ overcall shows an ordinary hand, so neither tells partner that a few cards from them make game or more. Double first, then bid spades: double-then-suit shows a hand too strong to overcall.

whyNot.1S: A simple overcall shows about 8-17 and an ordinary hand. Partner will pass with a few points, never guessing you can take nine tricks.
whyNot.2S: A jump overcall is weak: a long suit and little else.
whyNot.4S: A jump to game in an overcall is preemptive: long spades and a weak hand. Partner will pass with the ♥A and ♦KQ, and 6♠ makes.

problems.explanation: Partner's 1NT answers your double with about 6-10 points and a heart stopper. Now show the spades. Because you doubled first, bidding 4♠ shows a strong hand that can make game on its own, not a weak preempt, so partner knows the hand is worth more and can look for slam with good cards.

whyNot.2S: After doubling, a simple bid of your suit shows a good hand, but not one that makes game opposite almost nothing. You have about nine tricks.
whyNot.3N: With eight spades and a singleton heart, play in spades.
